analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the federal requirement that landlords give tenants 30 days' notice before starting an eviction.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would remove the federal 30-day notice requirement before eviction in federally assisted or backed housing, was introduced in February 2025 and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where it has seen no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 emergency, Congress added a rule that landlords in federally assisted or federally backed housing must give tenants 30 days' notice before starting an eviction. This bill would delete that rule, leaving eviction notice periods entirely up to state law. Tenant groups have long viewed the notice as an important protection for renters who live in public or federally subsidized housing.
analysis.who_benefits: Landlords who own federally assisted or federally backed rental housing — including owners of subsidized apartments and properties with federal mortgages — would no longer have to give tenants 30 days' notice before filing for eviction, and could proceed under whatever shorter notice state law allows.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the CARES Act provision requiring a 30-day notice period, so landlords in federally assisted or federally backed housing could begin eviction proceedings without the federally mandated 30-day notice.
It treats these evictions as a matter of state housing law, removing a uniform federal floor.

analysis.who_pays: Renters in federally assisted or federally backed housing would lose a guaranteed 30-day cushion before eviction proceedings begin — often the difference between catching up on rent and being taken to court. Those in states with weak tenant protections would have the least protection.

drawbacks.text: It removes a guaranteed 30-day notice before eviction proceedings in federally assisted or federally backed housing, so tenants could face eviction filings sooner after falling behind on rent.

Supporters argue the federal rule duplicates state law and that eviction procedures should be left to the states, as the bill's title suggests; but in states with weak tenant protections, that means less notice than tenants have now.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost falls entirely on renters: losing a guaranteed 30-day notice before eviction proceedings in federally backed housing, with nothing offered in return. The gain to landlords is modest convenience. On balance, the bill trades a meaningful protection for one of the most financially precarious groups for a small reduction in landlord paperwork, and the honest weighing comes out against it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Senator Hyde-Smith introduced the bill on February 6, 2025, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee.
No further action has been listed since the referral — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has happened, so tenants keep the 30-day notice protection for now. If the bill dies in committee, landlords who wanted the federal notice requirement removed will be the ones better off, without having to win a floor vote.

for.name: Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strike the CARES Act 30-day notice requirement.

for.name: Sen. Bill Hagerty
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-TN), original cosponsor at introduction
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction of the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 listed sponsors and cosponsors are Republicans; no Democrat has signed on.

industries.industry: Landlords and owners of federally assisted or federally backed rental housing
industries.note: They could start eviction proceedings without the federal 30-day notice, giving more flexibility against tenants who fall behind. Tenants lose the guaranteed notice window, which is often the only time they have to find money or new housing.

industries.industry: Federally backed rental housing operators (mortgage/loan programs with federal backing)
industries.note: The notice rule currently applies to any housing with a federal loan or federal backing; removing it simplifies operations for these owners. Renters in those same units lose a federal protection that state law may not replace.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee with no hearings or markup scheduled. Most bills referred to committee never reach the floor, and without movement from the committee chair it is unlikely to advance this Congress.
